title: | SABBATH AFTERNOON CLASS: Christ The Peacemaker: 1 God, 1 Nation, 12 Tribes

sense.text:
Today’s class is Christ the peacemaker: one God, one nation, twelve tribes, a continuation of a class taught the week before in Dallas.

“Who are called Uncircumcision by that which is called the Circumcision in the flesh made by hands”: this was a dis. To be called uncircumcised was a disrespect, and we come back to it later in the class.
“Aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise”, but now “ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.” It is through Christ’s blood.

“For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us”. Christ is our peace. Through his blood he broke down the middle wall of partition between us.

That middle wall of partition was the sacrificial law, the dividing of the nation, and it was symbolic of the veil in the tabernacle that separated the holy from the holiest of holies.

When did that wall get broken down? When Christ died. When he gave up the ghost the veil rent, symbolizing that he died for the whole nation of Israel. No longer did you have to go to the priests to get salvation; no longer did you have to go through them for sacrificing. That veil is what separated us from God, because God dwelt in the holiest of holies. Now the access way is through Christ: he’s the door now, for all Israel.

As we go through this class we’re going to study this enmity between the northern and southern kingdom: where it began, how they got to the point where they became enemies, what made them think that way, why Judah vexed Ephraim and why Ephraim envied Judah.

“Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances”. When Christ died it did away with the covenant we were under as far as animal sacrifice. That was the enmity: the northern kingdom left the laws and the southern kingdom continued within the law of animal sacrifice, and the hatred started between the two. The enmity was that sacrificial law, which would have prohibited the northern kingdom from salvation, because you would have had to be circumcised on the eighth day and come up in those rituals, and because they didn’t, it would have been a problem for them. The northern kingdom was being told they could no longer get into the kingdom.

“For to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace”: for Christ to make one new man of the two, he had to abolish in his flesh, in him dying, the enmity, the sacrificial law. The sacrificial law had to be destroyed to bring the nation of Israel back together. Otherwise there would always have been that division, why the southern kingdom would have been considered better, why the southern kingdom would have had the advantage. That tug and pull between Israel and Judah had to come to an end by Christ being our peace, dying for us and giving us all the opportunity.

precepts.why:
The veil in the tabernacle: “thou shalt make a vail of blue, and purple, and scarlet, and fine twined linen of cunning work”, hung “upon four pillars”, “overlaid with gold”, “their hooks shall be of gold, upon the four sockets of silver.” “That thou mayest bring in thither within the vail the ark of the testimony: and the vail shall divide unto you between the holy place and the most holy.”

The holy place was inside the tabernacle. The difference between the tabernacle and the temple: the temple was stationary; the tabernacle moved around when we were in the wilderness, built up and taken down as we moved. This veil is what separated the holy from the most holy, and that is the middle wall of partition in Ephesians 2:14.

“The priest, whom he shall anoint, and whom he shall consecrate to minister in the priest’s office in his father’s stead, shall make the atonement”, “for the holy sanctuary”, “for the tabernacle of the congregation, and for the altar”, “for the priests, and for all the people of the congregation.” “This shall be an everlasting statute unto you, to make an atonement for the children of Israel for all their sins once a year.”

Once a year the priest would go into the holiest of holies and sacrifice for the children of Israel for their sins. Behind that veil was the way to God, and only the priest went in.

When was the middle wall broken down? When Christ died. “Jesus, when he had cried again with a loud voice, yielded up the ghost. And, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom; and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent”.

When Christ gave up the ghost that veil rent, symbolizing that he died for the whole nation of Israel. No longer did you have to go to the priests to get salvation or go through them for sacrificing. The veil is what separated us from God, because God dwelt in the holiest of holies; now the access way is through Christ. He’s the door now for all Israel.

That’s why Christ said, “other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.”

It was always his plan to raise up other sheep: the scattered, the dispersed of Israel, had to be raised up. Him dying on the cross was to bring together in one the nation of Israel. That is how he made both one.

sense.text:
Let’s read about the ordinances. “The first covenant had also ordinances of divine service, and a worldly sanctuary”: the same ordinances we were reading about in Ephesians 2. The divine service was the different hand washings, the different ordinances concerning sacrificing.

We sacrificed twice a day every day of the week, and then had different sacrifices based on the sin, the free will offering, the high holy day. That’s why it says in Colossians let no man judge you in meat or drink or in respect of a holy day, because it was determined by the day, the high holy day, or by the infraction. Some people who were wealthy would offer up an oxen; if you were poor you might have offered up a turtle dove because you couldn’t afford an ox. There were different sacrifices based on the day, on the infraction, or on how God had blessed you.

“After the second veil, the tabernacle which is called the Holiest of all”. Inside the tabernacle the holiest of all was also called tabernacle, and there was a veil, a middle wall, that divided the holy from the most holy.

Symbolically, that is how Judah, the southern kingdom, looked upon themselves: the most holy. We still got to connect with God; we are different from you. Yeah, you Israel, but you ain’t really that. Yeah, you’re in the tabernacle, but you’re not right in the holiest of holies. That is the parallel.

“The priests went always into the first tabernacle, accomplishing the service of God. But into the second went the high priest alone once every year, not without blood, which he offered for himself, and for the errors of the people”. That is the holiest of holies where the priest went in.

“The Holy Ghost this signifying, that the way into the holiest of all was not yet made manifest”: the way to the holiest of all is the way to God, because God dwelt in the holiest of holies, and the way was not yet manifested.

What were they doing when they were sacrificing? They were rehearsing a righteous act, rehearsing what it meant to have a connection with God, so they would understand that there had to be a blood sacrifice for salvation. The Jews thought, because they had the blood sacrifice, that they were holier than the rest of the people. Christ said no: I’m going to come and die that perfect sacrifice to gather in one all the nation of Israel. That enmity, that pride the southern kingdom had starting with Judah, was that they were better, and God said no, you’re not: all of you have fallen, and through my grace all of you are going to be redeemed. We will go back into the Old Testament to understand why they thought like that.

“While as the first tabernacle was yet standing”: Christ, his blood and his dying for us, was not made manifest while the first tabernacle was standing. Even though Christ was crucified, resurrected and went back to the Father, that first tabernacle was still standing and people were still sacrificing. God was giving them a dispensation of time to be fully persuaded on him, and then it was going to be destroyed. Paul was preparing the Hebrews: get ready, this tabernacle is going to be destroyed, 70 A.D. When this falls you better be fully persuaded that Christ is the way, he is the door, he’s the way to God. The northern kingdom readily accepted that; the southern kingdom, many of them, had a problem with it. They didn’t believe the prophecies; even though they knew the laws, it didn’t connect.

“Which was a figure for the time then present”: that first tabernacle was a figure, “in which were offered both gifts and sacrifices, that could not make him that did the service perfect”. The sacrificial law was just rehearsing the righteous acts; it was never going to make them perfect, and this is what they struggled with. “As pertaining to the conscience”: as pertaining to your conscience.

“Which stood only in meats and drinks, and divers washings, and carnal ordinances”: that word ordinances again, which we read about in Ephesians. “Imposed on them until the time of reformation”: until the time of change, the ushering in of Christ and his blood. The blood of bulls and goats was not what was going to get us right.

“Christ being come an high priest of good things to come, by a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands”, “neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us.” If the blood of bulls and of goats sanctified to the purifying of the flesh, “how much more shall the blood of Christ”, who “offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?”

“And for this cause he is the mediator of the new testament”, the new agreement, “that by means of death, for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first testament”. Who was under the first testament? All twelve tribes of Israel. He died for all of them. Notice Paul has to write this to the Hebrews to get them on page.

“They which are called might receive the promise of eternal inheritance”: whoever was under the first testament, if they were called, would receive the promise of eternal inheritance. It doesn’t matter who was called, northern or southern kingdom; they would have the opportunity, with him being the high priest.

This is the advantage the southern kingdom had. “What advantage then hath the Jew?” What is the advantage of being a Jew? “Or what profit is there of circumcision?” What profit is there in being of the circumcision, being circumcised?

“Much every way”: every way you could think, it is profitable to be of the circumcision. “Chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God”: mainly because unto them were committed the oracles of God, the laws.

Committed: the word to use is give. Unto them were given the oracles of God. The laws were given to Judah, and what did God call Judah? The lawgiver. A lot of times we say wrongly that Levi was the lawgiver; Judah was the lawgiver.

precepts.why:
There is something in that same chapter that ties it back together: even though Judah, the southern kingdom, had the advantage, we were all the same. “For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God”.

Remember Paul is writing to the church in Rome; these are the scattered ones. Even though Judah were the lawgivers, we all have sinned. That is why the new testament is Christ dying for all those that were under the old testament: even though Judah and the southern kingdom had the laws, we all fall short.

That is the back and forth, the controversy between them, in Romans 11: all of a sudden the mystery is that the northern kingdom could be saved. Was that really a mystery back then?

sense.text: “Having made peace through the blood of his cross, by him to reconcile all things unto himself”: all twelve tribes.

“And you, that were sometime alienated and enemies in your mind by wicked works, yet now hath he reconciled”. He’s writing to the Colossians: you were once alienated, now you are reconciled. We read the same thing in Ephesians.

This is why reading is so important. Our people out in the world ain’t reading this Bible to understand; you have to read between the lines. Who’s the you? Those people who were sometimes called uncircumcised, the Gentiles. To be alienated means at one point you had to have been together. Reconciled means he brought them back. If you are reconciled, at one point in time you had to have been together, then went off, and then were brought back. This Bible from front to back is about us.

precepts.why:
“Whereof I am made a minister, according to the dispensation of God which is given to me for you, to fulfil the word of God”. What word is he going to fulfil? “Even the mystery which hath been hid from ages and from generations, but now is made manifest to his saints”.

For a long time it was hidden from the majority of people that the northern kingdom had a place. It wasn’t widely taught. Some people understood it, some of the scholars, but they still weren’t connecting the dots that the sacrificial law was going to be done away with and salvation was going to come through Christ. They read about the Messiah and knew he was to come, but they had sacrificed for so long that it was a mystery the northern kingdom was going to be ushered in: they’re uncircumcised, you had to do it on the eighth day, they haven’t been giving offerings for the atonement of their sin, they haven’t been keeping the day of atonement all these years, and now they’re going to come in?

Paul was one of those who understood the laws, and if he understood the laws he had to understand Christ. So why was he fighting against it? Because the dots weren’t connected. On the road Christ said, I’m that person you’re reading about, that’s me right there, and he said, that’s right, I know that scripture. At that moment he went out to teach. He didn’t have to confer with man, because he knew the scriptures already; his eyes were opened.

“To whom God would make known what is the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles; which is Christ in you, the hope of glory”. This is the riches of the glory of the mystery among the Gentiles: they are commonwealth together, they have one thing in common, and the wealth is Christ’s blood dying for them. Repentance is for them also. That’s why today, when brothers deal with these brothers talking about the northern kingdom of Israel and say, man, go sit down, that’s the same hatred in your spirit as your fathers: you reject them.

It was a mystery, but not to all. Some of the Jews understood; they just rejected it because they felt threatened. Their mind was to keep a division in the nation of Israel. They didn’t want them to come back together; they wanted to continue to shun them.

How could Paul’s eyes be opened and the northern kingdom’s eyes not be opened? Their eyes could be opened when their time came, and it wasn’t that time yet. That’s why he said, “Go not into the way of the Gentiles, and into any city of the Samaritans enter ye not: But go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”

Which lost sheep was he talking about? The ones right there in Jerusalem. They were lost; they didn’t understand him. Later on he told them to go to all nations, in Matthew 28, and in John 4 he went to Samaria. First he said, I’m going to start with you, because the laws were committed unto you. You rejected me; now I’m going to go to the Gentiles and use them to provoke you to jealousy.

sense.text:
Some of those learned men understood. Remember we read earlier in John 10: other sheep I have, which are not of this fold, them also must I bring, that there might be one fold and one shepherd.

“Then said the Jews among themselves, Whither will he go, that we shall not find him? will he go unto the dispersed among the Gentiles, and teach the Gentiles?” So they had to have understood. The word dispersed is in the Old Testament: Ezekiel is a good one, and Isaiah is the other. We will get to the Gentile part in a second.

“In the last day, that great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink. He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.”

precepts.why: “With the bread of understanding shall she feed him, and give him the water of wisdom to drink.” That water is referring to wisdom and understanding. He said, I will give you understanding: that is the living water.

“Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled.” If you hunger and thirst after righteousness, he said, I will give you that living water. That is what he told the woman at the well of Samaria.

sense.text: Christ “left Judea, and departed again into Galilee. And he must needs go through Samaria.” So now Christ is going up into Samaria. He told his apostles back in Matthew 10 not to enter Samaria, don’t go there, but now he is venturing up towards where the northern kingdom is at.

“How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me, which am a woman of Samaria? for the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans.” She is asking him: how are you asking me for drink when you Jews don’t have no dealings with us of Samaria, us Samaritans? As we read on you’re going to find she’s an Israelite, but the Jews didn’t deal with her, and later in the class we understand why they had that mentality.

But Christ knew better. Christ was dealing with her, and he taught his apostles to deal with them. Even so, Peter at one point pulled back, and Paul had to get on him, because of the mindset they had for so long, the enmity between them. It was hard for him to shake, and he knew that Christ dealt with them. They didn’t deal with them; they called them uncircumcised, and to be called uncircumcised was a disrespect.

“If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water.” What was the gift of God, what was hid for ages? This is for you also: if you thirst and hunger after righteousness, he said I’ll give you that living water of understanding, the keys to understanding how to be saved. And it’s not going to come by you coming from Samaria down to Jerusalem sacrificing.

I’m going to tear apart that enmity that divides you, where they will no longer think they won’t have no dealings with you. I’m going to give understanding to Peter, that what I’ve made clean, don’t call common anymore. I’m going to send Paul to teach the people and bring them to repentance. You’re going to have some Jews that fight against it, but the prophecy is the two shall be one. So he’s telling her: I will give you living water, you’re going to understand.

“Art thou greater than our father Jacob, which gave us the well”: she is making it clear. She’s letting you know, I’m part of Israel, I’m a descendant of the Israelites, but you Jews don’t deal with us, you have no dealings with us.

Put your mind in there: you being a Jew coming up like that, you see me and it’s ‘we ain’t dealing with that.’ That’s Judah vexing Ephraim: heathen, gentile, uncircumcised. No, he said, if you thirst after this I’ll give you what you’ll never thirst again: I’ll give you the understanding of these scriptures.

“Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again: But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.” That’s the kingdom. That’s the water he is offering up to her.

“A devout man, and one that feared God with all his house, which gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway.” This man was a devout man, and being devout means you are keeping the commandments. God blesses the man that thirsts after righteousness, and that was Cornelius.
Because he was like that, look what it says next: “He saw in a vision evidently about the ninth hour of the day”. Who did the vision come from? From God.

precepts.why:
Having a vision from God: “And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions”. If God is going to pour his spirit upon you and deal with you, you better be thirsting after righteousness.

Remember, Cornelius was up with the northern kingdom, he was up with Rome, yet God’s spirit was upon him. He was a devout man that feared God. He’s keeping the commandments, he’s getting visions from God, he got the spirit. And trust me, the Jews understood Joel 2: that means God’s spirit is upon him.

So as a Jew, raised in the laws, knowing ‘we don’t deal with these people’, them people are the riff raff, what would be your reaction when you see somebody coming in devout to the commandments, explaining the visions God gave him, and you say God put a spirit upon him based on Joel? You’d be shocked.

Stay in the same chapter: “While Peter yet spake these words, the Holy Ghost fell on all them which heard the word. And they of the circumcision which believed were astonished, as many as came with Peter, because that on the Gentiles also was poured out the gift of the Holy Ghost.”

They were astonished, saying damn, they got the holy spirit. These were Jews that believed, but they were shocked to see the northern kingdom: how the hell they got the spirit too? So you telling me all that sacrifice we’ve been doing all those years, and they just got the holy spirit too? God, that’s not how it goes. What about the temple, the high priest, the ram, all the diverse washings I’ve learned? We don’t have no dealings with them.

sense.text: Paul and Barnabas “persuaded them to continue in the grace of God.” Paul and Barnabas are on fire, persuading the people. “And the next sabbath day came almost the whole city together to hear the word of God”: the whole city comes out, because Paul and Barnabas were on fire persuading these people, gathering the twelve tribes of Israel together.

“But when the Jews saw the multitudes, they were filled with envy, and spake against those things which were spoken by Paul, contradicting and blaspheming.” Them Jews were those Pharisees, a lot of them, and they did not want the joining of the twelve tribes of Israel together. Like today, you’re going to see it: they want to keep that division.

They were filled with envy. The many that were astonished, you don’t think they went back and told it: ‘I saw this guy,’ ‘nah, that can’t be.’ Here comes the plot, because they could not accept the northern kingdom. Even though, as we read when we go into the Old Testament, it kept on saying it, they were blinded for a purpose.

“It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you”. Remember he told them in Matthew 10:5-6 to go not in the way of the gentiles, not into Samaria, but rather go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Them in Jerusalem were hearing the word; the southern kingdom was getting the word, but you had many that were rejecting it.

Whither will he go, to the dispersed among the gentiles, and teach the gentiles? That’s where he’s going to go. “But seeing ye put it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life, lo, we turn to the Gentiles.” Now we’re turning to the northern kingdom.

“Wherefore remember, that ye being in time past Gentiles in the flesh, who are called Uncircumcision by that which is called the Circumcision in the flesh made by hands”. He said remember, you were called uncircumcised. Remember that, but you’re no longer uncircumcised. You’re now part of the commonwealth of Israel, and now that you are part of the commonwealth of Israel you better not boast.

In times past he was called uncircumcised, heathen, gentile, by that which was of the circumcision.

“That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world”. Back then they were saying he was without hope, he was without God, he wasn’t part of the commonwealth.
“But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.” Now you’re brought into the fold through Christ’s blood; now you’re being brought back into the fold.

“For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us”. He’s made all peace; we are both one. He has broken down the middle wall of partition that was between us by his blood, him dying. “Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace”: so he’s bringing us back together.

precepts.why: Jump up to verse 9: “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” Not of the works you did, lest any man should boast, because remember, we all fall short. So now he’s telling the northern kingdom: now that you’re brought in, don’t become boastful, don’t become prideful. You’re part of this commonwealth now.

Being called uncircumcised was a derogatory term. “Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will punish all them which are circumcised with the uncircumcised”: I’m going to punish all those that are circumcised with the uncircumcised. “Egypt, and Judah, and Edom, and the children of Ammon, and Moab, and all that are in the utmost corners, that dwell in the wilderness: for all these nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in the heart.”

So to be called uncircumcised was a derogatory thing, because they were joined unto dumb idols.

“Ye know that ye were Gentiles, carried away unto these dumb idols, even as ye were led.” You were gentiles carried away unto these dumb idols; you were called uncircumcised. That’s why the Jews didn’t have no dealings with you.

sense.text:
Listen to what Tobit is saying in his prayer: “For he doth scourge, and hath mercy: he leadeth down to hell, and bringeth up again”. God scourges and has mercy. Where do we read that in the Old Testament concerning the northern kingdom, God punishing but having mercy? It doesn’t use those words, but Hosea is the book.

“Neither is there any that can avoid his hand”: all of us are going to catch that, nobody can avoid his hand. He’s going to destroy and scourge, and he did that. He scourged, but he did have mercy.

“Confess him before the Gentiles, ye children of Israel”. He said go confess him before the gentiles. This is a prayer. Isn’t that what we’re doing today? Isn’t that what they did back then? Matthew 28: go into all nations and preach. Confess him before the gentiles, “for he hath scattered us among them.”

“There declare his greatness, and extol him before all the living”. “And he will scourge us for our iniquities, and will have mercy again, and will gather us out of all nations, among whom he hath scattered us.” He will have mercy again, and he is going to gather: don’t we read that in Isaiah 11?

“If ye turn to him with your whole heart, and with your whole mind, and deal uprightly before him, then will he turn unto you, and will not hide his face from you.” “In the land of my captivity do I praise him, and declare his might and majesty to a sinful nation. O ye sinners, turn and do justice before him”. “I will extol my God, and my soul shall praise the King of heaven, and shall rejoice in his greatness.” That’s repentance.

precepts.why:
God scourges and has mercy on the northern kingdom: “Yet the number of the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured nor numbered; and it shall come to pass, that in the place where it was said unto them, Ye are not my people”. This is referring to the northern kingdom. “There it shall be said unto them, Ye are the sons of the living God.”

So they’re going to be scourged, but then they’re going to be brought back in. It was always prophesied. For some reason that scripture eluded many people’s minds. It was the job of the leaders to tell the people, and a lot of them didn’t say nothing; they left those prophecies alone.

There was going to come a point where they were not going to be called God’s people. They were going to be called gentiles, or heathens; there were other names that were given. But it says there you shall be called the sons of the living God.

This was Nebuchadnezzar, but read it anyway as an example of the Lord coming in and destroying. The captain of the guard, a servant of the king of Babylon, came unto Jerusalem: “And he burnt the house of the Lord, and the king’s house, and all the houses of Jerusalem, and every great man’s house burnt he with fire.” That’s the scourge we just read about in Tobit.

“And all the army of the Chaldees, that were with the captain of the guard, brake down the walls of Jerusalem round about.” And the rest of the people that were left in the city, and the fugitives that fell away to the king of Babylon, “with the remnant of the multitude”, the captain of the guard carried away. He scourged, but he did have mercy.

The same thing Tobit said, that he will gather you out of all nations: “And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people”. “And he shall set up an ensign for the nations, and shall assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.”

Then the last part: “The envy also of Ephraim shall depart, and the adversaries of Judah shall be cut off: Ephraim shall not envy Judah, and Judah shall not vex Ephraim.” When he gathers them, that enmity between the northern kingdom and the southern kingdom comes to an end.

sense.text: “When at the first he lightly afflicted the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, and afterward did more grievously afflict her”. He began to afflict the northern kingdom lightly, but then he became more severe with his affliction on them.

Why were they prideful? Why could they not humble down with all this affliction? Look at what it says in the chapter: “The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light”. “For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.” This is referring to Christ.

“Of the increase of his government and peace there shall be no end, upon the throne of David, and upon his kingdom, to order it, and to establish it with judgment and with justice from henceforth even for ever.” This king that’s going to come is going to come out of where? From henceforth and for ever, it was going to come out of the line of Judah. “The zeal of the Lord of hosts will perform this.”

This was a prophecy foretold, and they heard it and didn’t like it, that the messiah was coming out of Judah.

“The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it hath lighted upon Israel.” Even in the affliction, look at their response: “even Ephraim and the inhabitant of Samaria, that say in the pride and stoutness of heart, The bricks are fallen down, but we will build with hewn stones: the sycomores are cut down, but we will change them into cedars.” “Therefore the Lord shall set up the adversaries”: because of their pride he’s going to send their enemies against them.

Because they didn’t like that prophecy, God said I’m going to send the Assyrians against you. And keep in mind what happened before that with Jeroboam, how they dealt with them: they became an animosity group between them.

“Manasseh, Ephraim; and Ephraim, Manasseh: and they together shall be against Judah. For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still.” He said Ephraim and Manasseh are going to be against you. They don’t like them, and now they got to hear that the messiah is coming out of them. Nah, they got pride; they didn’t want to hear it.

precepts.why:
Go back a little bit in the history. In the six and thirtieth year of the reign of Asa, the king of Israel “came up against Judah”, and built, “to the intent that he might let none go out or come in to Asa king of Judah.” He laid a siege.

Then Asa brought silver and gold “out of the treasures of the house of the Lord and of the king’s house”, and sent to the king of Syria that dwelt at Damascus: “There is a league between me and thee, as there was between my father and thy father: behold, I have sent thee silver and gold; go, break thy league with” the king of Israel, “that he may depart from me.” The king of Syria hearkened unto king Asa, “and sent the captains of his armies against the cities of Israel”, and smote “all the store cities of Naphtali.” And the king of Israel “left off building”, “and let his work cease.”

So the northern kingdom came against the southern kingdom, and we made a league with them and said, listen, get them off of us. That shows you how strong the northern kingdom was: it was ten tribes. They started encroaching down towards the land, and we paid them off, and guess what, they ran them out. Here’s the enmity between them: they continued to try to uproot Judah.

Remember what we read in Isaiah 9. In the days of Ahaz king of Judah, the king of Syria and the king of Israel “went up toward Jerusalem to war against it, but could not prevail against it. And it was told the house of David, saying, Syria is confederate with Ephraim. And his heart was moved, and the heart of his people, as the trees of the wood are moved with the wind.”

The Lord sent Isaiah to meet Ahaz and say unto him, “Take heed, and be quiet; fear not, neither be fainthearted for the two tails of these smoking firebrands”, because they “have taken evil counsel against thee, saying, Let us go up against Judah, and vex it, and let us make a breach therein for us”. “Thus saith the Lord God, It shall not stand, neither shall it come to pass.” “Within threescore and five years shall Ephraim be broken, that it be not a people.”

So now they made a league with Syria to come against us, and God said don’t worry about them: sixty-five years from now Israel won’t even be a people. That’s why when you get to the New Testament, in John 4, she says you Jews have no dealings with us: because we looked at them like they weren’t a people no more. And that’s when we made a league with Syria, and that caused a lot of controversy.

So how do we, as one nation, get so far that now we’re warring against each other? Go back into the history, so that when we get to the New Testament you understand that enmity, that God had to send his Son to die for us to stop all that, because without his blood coming, the Jews always saw themselves better.

sense.text:
How did we get from one nation to warring against each other? What happened before to bring about those feelings? Go back into the history, so that when we get to the New Testament you understand the enmity God had to send his Son to die for, to stop all that, because without his blood coming the Jews always saw themselves better. Give me something disrespectful that Judah did: take me to 1 Kings 12, where he said “my little finger shall be thicker than my father’s loins.”

“And Rehoboam went to Shechem”, and all Israel came to make him king. Jeroboam the son of Nebat was yet in Egypt, “for he was fled from the presence of king Solomon”, and they sent and called him, and he and all the congregation of Israel came and spake unto Rehoboam.

“Thy father made our yoke grievous.” Solomon made the yoke of the kingdom grievous; he worked them. How do you think he built the Lord’s temple and his palaces and all his stuff? He had men singers and everything, he had them working. When they went to harvest the wood, they went over into another king’s land and spent six months there at a time, away from their family, away from their land, raising crops for the king’s service. So they said, listen, your father made our yoke grievous; all we’re asking is for you to ease up on us a little bit, “and we will serve thee.”

Rehoboam sent them away three days and consulted with the old men that stood before Solomon, and they told him, “If thou wilt be a servant unto this people this day, and wilt serve them, and answer them, and speak good words to them, then they will be thy servants for ever.” But he forsook the counsel of the old men and consulted with the young men that were grown up with him.

The young men told him to say, “My little finger shall be thicker than my father’s loins.” Now wrap your mind around it: Jeroboam was a full-grown man, he was no boy; he worked for Solomon. Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, has come into his position, and the way it reads, Rehoboam was a younger man than Jeroboam. You told this man, my little finger’s gonna be bigger than my father’s penis, that’s how I’m gonna afflict you. What do you think you’re gonna get out of that? That’s open disrespect, said to all of them, and it helped build that animosity. Why would you say something so rude to him, showing no regard? Think about the pride Jeroboam had now: how he came up, his family line, his name. These were mighty men too, and somebody tells you, my finger will be bigger than my father’s penis. How you like that?

“My father hath chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.”

Jeroboam and all the people came the third day, “And the king answered the people roughly, and forsook the old men’s counsel”, and spake after the counsel of the young men. “Wherefore the king hearkened not unto the people; for the cause was from the Lord, that he might perform his saying”, which the Lord spake by Ahijah the Shilonite unto Jeroboam.

“What portion have we in David?” So what portion do we have now? “Neither have we inheritance in the son of Jesse: to your tents, O Israel: now see to thine own house, David.” Everybody to your tents: they were dissing us. So Israel departed unto their tents.

Rehoboam reigned over the children of Israel which dwelt in the cities of Judah. Then he sent Adoram, who was over the tribute, “and all Israel stoned him with stones, that he died.” Rehoboam sent somebody to try to go get the tribute money, and they were like, are you crazy? They killed him, man, stoned him: you ain’t getting nothing. It showed you the power … had.

Imagine the fighting and the problems after this. It carried on for generations: that your great-great-grandfather told my great-great-grandfather about his dick. We needed a peacemaker to come and end it.

“And Hezekiah sent to all Israel and Judah, and wrote letters also to Ephraim and Manasseh, that they should come to the house of the Lord at Jerusalem, to keep the passover.” Look what Hezekiah was trying to do: he was trying to bring them back together. The kingdom split; let’s just try to work this out, come back down and keep the feasts.

precepts.why:
The posts went from city to city through the country of Ephraim and Manasseh even unto Zebulun, “but they laughed them to scorn, and mocked them.” Hell no, we ain’t coming back, we ain’t messing with you, you act like we nobody. We done stoned a man; no, we ain’t coming back.

That is the mocking that answered Hezekiah’s call to the feast. So why would Ephraim, the northern kingdom, be so prideful in their own history, feeling they’ve got a stake? It goes back to Joseph: his brothers sold him into slavery in Egypt, he gained power under Pharaoh, and as the prophecy in Genesis said, his brothers came to him for help without knowing he was their brother.

sense.text: “Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age.” The sons felt a way because Joseph was his baby: he showed him love, that’s my baby boy. So the brothers were vexed about that, and then “he made him a coat of many colours.”
When his brethren saw that their father loved him more than all of them, “they hated him, and could not speak peaceably unto him.” You see that envy coming right there.

Joseph dreamed a dream and told it his brethren, “and they hated him yet the more.” Their sheaves “stood round about, and made obeisance to my sheaf”: they all bowed to me, he said, in my dream these sheaves, all of you bow to me. And they said, “Shalt thou indeed reign over us? or shalt thou indeed have dominion over us?” And they hated him yet the more “for his dreams, and for his words.”

Then “the sun and the moon and the eleven stars made obeisance to me.” He told it to his father and his brethren, and his father rebuked him: “Shall I and thy mother and thy brethren indeed come to bow down ourselves to thee to the earth?” Wait a second, your mother and father and all your brothers, we all gonna bow to you?

“And his brethren envied him”: now they hated him and they envied him. “But his father observed the saying”: the father said, what the hell you talking about, but let me consider what’s being said. This is the beginning of the hatred between them.

At the end of that history they all came into Egypt and had to bow to Joseph, because he controlled the food; if it wasn’t for Joseph they would all have died. So try being from the tribe of Ephraim and Manasseh, and you hear the history of the father of your tribe, Joseph, and you know that through your father all the twelve tribes of Israel were saved. That’s the level of pride. For Judah, the pride is that the Messiah came out of their tribe; for Benjamin, Paul. Every tribe has something it holds on to, to say we were mighty men. And for Ephraim and Manasseh the heritage is, yo, we were mighty, we saved all Israel.

“Joseph is a fruitful bough, even a fruitful bough by a well; whose branches run over the wall.” The archers hated him and shot at him, “But his bow abode in strength, and the arms of his hands were made strong by the hands of the mighty God of Jacob.” He is blessed “with blessings of heaven above, blessings of the deep that lieth under”: Joseph was getting blessed.

“The blessings of thy father have prevailed above the blessings of my progenitors unto the utmost bound of the everlasting hills: they shall be on the head of Joseph, and on the crown of the head of him that was separate from his brethren.” This crown is going to be upon the head of Joseph, the one separated from his brethren. So they read the prophecy and say, there’s going to be a crown upon our head, we’re somebody, we great: why are we being treated like this? Why are we treated like nothing, ‘why we got ten parts in David’? All of this helped build that animosity.

What Joseph forgot, what he wasn’t accepting, is back in the chapter: “Judah, thou art he whom thy brethren shall praise”, “thy father’s children shall bow down before thee.” We all had to realize what that scripture says: we were all going to bow down. This is future prophecy.
“Judah is a lion’s whelp”, “he stooped down, he couched as a lion, and as an old lion; who shall rouse him up?”

Here’s the point: “The sceptre shall not depart from Judah”. Regardless of what anybody do, the rulership shall not depart from Judah, “nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be.” Unto Christ our King from the tribe of Judah is the gathering of the people. That’s why Zechariah says the tents of Judah first. That’s what we all had to accept, and it was hard to digest.

“Moreover he refused the tabernacle of Joseph, and chose not the tribe of Ephraim.” Why would he have refused the tabernacle of Joseph? Why did Joseph feel his tabernacle was something in the first place, so that God had to come back and make clear he was refusing it? For God to have to refuse it, there had to have been something Joseph felt his tabernacle was worthy of, to be called the tabernacle where men sacrifice: Joseph, for them, was trying to push that.

precepts.why:
Going backwards to the New Testament: “Our fathers worshipped in this mountain; and ye say, that in Jerusalem is the place where men ought to worship.” The woman at the well was saying our fathers worshipped in this mountain, and you say Jerusalem is the place. They were worshipping in the mountains of Ephraim in the northern kingdom.

When we first came into the land, where was the first altar set up? Mount Gerizim, mount Ebal: that’s the land of Samaria. So when the nation split, they said, we’re going to go back and worship where we were first, where God first ordained it. But then God had to come next and make clear that’s not the place he chose, even though you sacrificed there.

And Christ had to come back and say, neither this mountain nor Jerusalem: I’m going to lay all this flat. Jerusalem, you ain’t going to be special, and whatever you think you’ve got going on here ain’t going to be special either; it’s going to be desolate. I am the way.

“Then Joshua built an altar unto the Lord God of Israel in mount Ebal, As Moses the servant of the Lord commanded the children of Israel”, “an altar of whole stones, over which no man hath lift up any iron”, and they offered burnt offerings and “sacrificed peace offerings.” He wrote upon the stones “a copy of the law of Moses”.

All Israel, their elders, officers and judges stood on this side the ark and on that side, “half of them over against mount Gerizim, and half of them over against mount Ebal”. So when they first came to the land they were sacrificing in those mountains, and that was ordained of God. That is why the northern kingdom felt justified in their mind: we know we can sacrifice here. But that’s not the place God chose.

“But I have chosen Jerusalem, that my name might be there; and have chosen David to be over my people Israel.” He had to make it clear, I’ve chosen Jerusalem, so that people would know why he refused the tabernacle of Joseph: it’s not in Ephraim, it’s the city of Jerusalem, the city of David, where I’m putting my name.

You understand now why they had that thinking. All this brought about the thought that they had a place too, a name that was worthy. And it’s not that it wasn’t, but at the end of the day God was choosing Judah, and that’s where the schism began.

sense.text: Try to understand, when Hosea proclaimed what he was about to proclaim, the mentality of the people and how they thought. “I will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and will cause to cease the kingdom of the house of Israel.” Think about us hearing this: the kingdom of the house of Israel is going to come to an end. That means they’re no more, and we’re not. “I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel.”

“Call her name Lo–ruhamah: for I will no more have mercy upon the house of Israel; but I will utterly take them away.” We hear this and say, well, they’re going to cease and they’re going to be taken away.

“But I will have mercy upon the house of Judah, and will save them by the Lord their God, and will not save them by bow, nor by sword, nor by battle, by horses, nor by horsemen.” We hear he’s going to save Judah: we good.

“Call his name Lo–ammi: for ye are not my people, and I will not be your God.” When they heard God say you are not my people and I am not your God, that’s why, when we get to John 4, it says ‘you Jews don’t have dealings with us’: you see us as Gentiles, you don’t deal with us.

That was the enmity that separated us. We were still sacrificing and keeping the laws, and we looked down at the northern kingdom as nothing. God said that enmity has to cease, that sacrificial law has to be done away: I’m going to die for all of you and give you a place back. But there were Jews who were not accepting that. That was the mentality back then.

“Hath God cast away his people? God forbid. For I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.” Look at Paul writing to the church in Rome: has God cast away his people? No. Why would the northern kingdom think we’d been cast away? Because the Holy Spirit jumped on them, and it was said, we’re going to turn to the Gentiles now. But I’m of that: God didn’t cast us away, I’m part of that. Don’t become too prideful now; yeah, the spirit is on you, just remember we all fall short.

“God hath not cast away his people which he foreknew.” Elias made intercession against Israel: “Lord, they have killed thy prophets, and digged down thine altars; and I am left alone, and they seek my life.” And God answered, “I have reserved to myself seven thousand men, who have not bowed the knee to the image of Baal.”

So he’s telling the northern kingdom: even though you may not see them, the southern kingdom, Judah, is still alive; there are still men reserved to him. In their mind there’s nobody left. Look what happened with Cornelius: it astonished the people, the Jews didn’t believe it, they were vexed and had envy that God was dealing with them. He said, just know there are men reserved who have not bowed a knee.
“Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace.” There’s a remnant of Judah that’s going to come back.

“Have they stumbled that they should fall? God forbid: but rather through their fall salvation is come unto the Gentiles, for to provoke them to jealousy.” That would provoke the southern kingdom to jealousy: this dude was wearing a toga last year, celebrating Bacchus or whatever he was doing, and now the Holy Spirit is on him and he’s prophesying, and we’re like, damn, we’ve got to get ourselves together. That was the prophecy, that it will provoke them.

“Now if the fall of them be the riches of the world, and the diminishing of them the riches of the Gentiles; how much more their fulness? For I speak to you Gentiles, inasmuch as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, I magnify mine office”. Peter’s office was to the circumcision; Paul’s was to the uncircumcised. It makes sense: Paul could not prophesy to the circumcision, they would have killed him, because he was one of them. You’ve got to go far out, Paul, go teach some people out there, and he was more than capable.

Who else should have been capable? All those Hebrews should have been capable, but they didn’t understand Christ. They needed someone to teach them again the first principles of the oracles of God; they didn’t need strong meat, they needed milk, simple things like Deuteronomy 18:18 and Isaiah 56. The Bible was always prophesying of him.

“If by any means I may provoke to emulation them which are my flesh, and might save some of them.” “For if the casting away of them be the reconciling of the world”: the falling of the southern kingdom is the reconciling. To reconcile is to bring back together all the tribes; you needed them to fall to bring them back. “What shall the receiving of them be, but life from the dead?”
“For if the firstfruit be holy, the lump is also holy”: if Christ is holy, he’s the firstfruit, and the lump is also holy. “And if the root be holy, so are the branches.”

“And if some of the branches be broken off, and thou, being a wild olive tree, wert graffed in among them”. The wild olive tree is the scattered Israelites that were living like Gentiles; they’re now being grafted back in. Breaking out these precepts is too long for today; Romans 11 is for next week.

The point: “Boast not against the branches. But if thou boast, thou bearest not the root, but the root thee.” You coming in now, don’t boast against the natural branches, because they were keeping the law; they were falling short on understanding Christ, but you were worshipping another god. I’m calling you both out: ain’t none of you right, all of you have fallen short. We needed Christ to come and die to remove all that away from all of us: our dealings towards the northern kingdom, the northern kingdom feeling isolated, the disdain and the hatred they had. And Christ said, my blood is what’s going to redeem all of you, to bring you back.
